 Tumour-Intrinsic STING Activation Delays Brain Metastasis and Improves Breast Cancer Survival
 by 
 November 16, 2026 
 in 
 Cancer , Health 
 Reading Time: 3 mins read
 0 
 Tumour-Intrinsic STING Activation Delays Brain Metastasis and Improves Breast Cancer Survival
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 Tumour-intrinsic activation of Stimulator of Interferon Genes is significantly associated with favourable long-term prognosis and delayed brain metastasis development in breast cancer patients, according to new research. Investigating the pathway via phosphorylated STING as an activation marker, investigators uncovered that STING exerts direct regulatory roles within cancer cells distinct from its established function in immune cell stimulation.
 Stimulator of Interferon Genes, known as STING, is recognized as a key inducer of type I interferon signalling that promotes immune cell activation and antitumour immune responses. Although reduced STING expression has been reported across multiple tumour types, leading to investigations of STING agonists to elicit anti-tumour immune responses in triple-negative breast cancer, the specific role of STING activation within the tumour cells themselves had remained largely unexplored.
 To determine how tumour-intrinsic STING activation influences breast cancer progression and metastatic spread, the researchers examined phosphorylated STING expression by immunohistochemistry across two independent clinical cohorts. The primary breast cancer clinical cohort consisted of 546 breast cancer tumours evaluated with more than 25 years of clinical follow-up, providing an extensive timeline to evaluate long-term breast cancer–specific survival outcomes.
 The study also assessed a distinct breast cancer to brain metastasis cohort consisting of 81 brain metastasis tumours, which included 50 matched breast cancer and brain metastasis tumour pairs. Alongside clinical tissue evaluation, the research team conducted quantitative proteomic profiling following STING overexpression and knockdown in triple-negative breast cancer cells to define the intrinsic biological programs governed by STING activation.
 The clinical analyses revealed that low or absent phosphorylated STING expression in primary tumours was significantly associated with poorer breast cancer–specific survival. This association was statistically significant at both 5 years (P = 0.0009) and 30 years (P < 0.001) of clinical follow-up, highlighting that the absence of intrinsic pathway activation correlates with inferior survival over decades.
 When examining metastatic progression, the investigators observed that patients whose primary tumours exhibited high phosphorylated STING expression experienced a significantly longer time to brain metastasis development (P = 0.0112). In contrast, phosphorylated STING expression was not associated with patient survival following brain metastasis surgery, indicating that the protective association is specifically tied to delaying the initial formation of distant brain metastases.
 Integrative network and pathway analyses of the quantitative proteomic data revealed coordinated biological reprogramming within triple-negative breast cancer cells upon STING modulation. Pathway alterations included the upregulation of ribosomal and translational machinery, accompanied by the suppression of metabolic programs and programs associated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition.
 Together, these observations demonstrate that tumour-intrinsic STING activation is linked to favourable prognosis, delayed brain metastasis progression, and coordinated proteomic reprogramming. The study authors concluded that these findings highlight a crucial tumour-intrinsic dimension of STING biology beyond immune activation alone, noting that defining these intrinsic cellular effects is critical for effectively exploiting STING-targeted therapeutic pathways in breast cancer.

 Article Title: STING beyond immunity: tumour-intrinsic roles in breast cancer progression and metastasis
